patient.name: Sinéad Okafor
patient.complaint: Tingling around the mouth and cramping hands the day after neck surgery
background: Large multinodular goitre causing pressure symptoms

diagnosis.exam: Expect 'Which is the most likely diagnosis?' after neck surgery with tingling and spasm, or a bloods pattern separating hypo, pseudo and pseudopseudo.

points: Day 1 after **total thyroidectomy** for a large multinodular goitre.
Tingling around her **mouth** and in her fingertips since this morning.
Now her hands are cramping into claws.

steps.lead: Sinéad's neck surgery is the commonest adult cause: **thyroidectomy** can bruise, devascularise or remove the parathyroids.
No PTH means **low calcium, high phosphate** and irritable nerves and muscles: exactly what Sinéad is feeling.
Perioral **paraesthesia**, **carpopedal spasm**, brisk reflexes and a fresh neck scar: hypocalcaemia after neck surgery.

steps.q: The FY1 taps in front of Sinéad's ear and her upper lip twitches. What is this sign?
steps.r: **Chvostek's**: tapping the facial nerve over the parotid. Trousseau's is carpal spasm with a BP cuff.

steps.lead: Sinéad has a positive **Chvostek's**; inflating a BP cuff above systolic would provoke **Trousseau's** carpal spasm too.
Sinéad's hands are normal and her PTH will be low. **Short metacarpals** with a high PTH would mean **pseudohypoparathyroidism**.

steps.text: A low calcium with a **high** PTH is not hypoparathyroidism. Think vitamin D deficiency (secondary hyperparathyroidism) or pseudohypoparathyroidism.

investigation.exam: Expect the bone profile with PTH (low calcium, high phosphate, low PTH), checking magnesium, and the ECG (prolonged QT).

steps.title: Bloods, day 1 post-op
steps.text: Low calcium, high phosphate, **low PTH**: the parathyroids have stopped working.

visual.title: Adjusted calcium
visual.label: Sinéad 1.71
visual.caption: Below about 1.9 with symptoms is severe: treat now.

steps.lead: Bone profile plus PTH makes the diagnosis. Sinéad's **magnesium** and **vitamin D** are normal, so they are not the cause.

steps.q: What else must be done urgently for Sinéad?
steps.r: Hypocalcaemia **prolongs the QT** and risks arrhythmia; an ECG is needed now.

visual.title: QTc on Sinéad's ECG
visual.label: Sinéad 498 ms
visual.caption: Sinus tachycardia with a **long QT**: the ECG clue to low calcium.

steps.lead: Sinéad's ECG shows a **prolonged QT**; renal function and 25-hydroxyvitamin D complete the screen.

steps.text: Always check **magnesium** in hypocalcaemia: low magnesium blocks PTH release and calcium will not correct until it is replaced.

management.exam: Expect 'immediate management' of symptomatic hypocalcaemia (IV calcium gluconate) and long-term active vitamin D with calcium.

steps.q: Sinéad has carpopedal spasm, calcium 1.71 and a long QT. What is the immediate treatment?
steps.r: **Symptomatic** severe hypocalcaemia needs **IV calcium gluconate** on a cardiac monitor. Oral routes are too slow.

steps.lead: Sinéad fits the notes' example exactly: post-thyroidectomy, carpopedal spasm, Chvostek's positive. **IV calcium gluconate** first; oral calcium is for mild cases.
Tetany, seizures, laryngospasm or a long QT make it an **emergency**: Sinéad is treated on a monitored bed.

visual.title: Sinéad's calcium
visual.caption: IV gluconate lifts it; alfacalcidol plus oral calcium keeps it up.

steps.title: Treating hypocalcaemia
nodes: Yes → IV calcium gluconate, cardiac monitoring
Then oral calcium + active vitamin D

steps.lead: Sinéad goes home on **alfacalcidol** plus oral calcium, with calcium checks as her glands may recover over weeks.

steps.text: Plain **colecalciferol** needs PTH-driven 1-alpha-hydroxylation to work. Without PTH, give **active** vitamin D: alfacalcidol or calcitriol.

science.exam: Expect mechanisms: why phosphate is high, why low calcium causes tetany, or why PTH is high in pseudohypoparathyroidism.

steps.lead: Without PTH, Sinéad loses bone resorption, renal calcium reabsorption and vitamin D activation, and her kidneys **keep phosphate**.
Sinéad's low extracellular calcium **lowers the threshold** for depolarisation, so her nerves fire spontaneously: tingling and spasm.
Sinéad's parathyroids sit behind the thyroid and were **damaged or removed** during her thyroidectomy.
In **pseudohypoparathyroidism** the glands work but the tissues ignore PTH (a **GNAS** G-protein defect), so PTH is high and calcium low.

steps.q: A child has short 4th metacarpals, low calcium and high PTH. Which defect is most likely?
steps.r: End-organ resistance via a G-protein (**GNAS**) defect: **pseudohypoparathyroidism**.

steps.lead: If Sinéad's glands never recover, chronic hypocalcaemia risks seizures, arrhythmias, **laryngospasm** and **cataracts**.

mcq.q: What is the most common cause of hypoparathyroidism in adults?

o: Carpal spasm with a BP cuff
Facial twitch on tapping over the facial nerve
mcq.r: Tap over the **parotid**; Trousseau's is the cuff.

o: Inflating a BP cuff above systolic
mcq.r: Carpal spasm from ischaemia of irritable nerves.

mcq.q: Low calcium with HIGH PTH and short metacarpals suggests?

o: High calcium, low phosphate, high PTH
Low calcium, high phosphate, low PTH
Low calcium, low phosphate, high PTH
Normal calcium, normal phosphate, normal PTH
mcq.r: No PTH: calcium falls, phosphate retained.

mcq.q: Which ECG change does hypocalcaemia cause?
What is the emergency treatment of symptomatic hypocalcaemia?
Which vitamin D is used long-term in hypoparathyroidism?
mcq.r: **Active** vitamin D (alfacalcidol or calcitriol) bypasses the need for PTH.

mcq.q: Why is phosphate high in hypoparathyroidism?
o: Loss of PTH-driven renal phosphate excretion
mcq.r: PTH normally makes the kidney **excrete** phosphate.
A **G-protein** signalling defect causing PTH resistance.

Trousseau's: BP cuff above systolic causes carpal spasm

points.p: Correct magnesium and vitamin D deficiency; treat the cause

prompts.tip: Exam thinking: bone, kidney, vitamin D.

points.p: Loss of bone resorption, renal calcium reabsorption and 1-alpha-hydroxylation
Loss of renal phosphate excretion: high phosphate
Low calcium lowers the depolarisation threshold: tetany, paraesthesia, seizures

prompts.q: Why does thyroidectomy cause it, why is PTH high in pseudohypoparathyroidism, and what are the complications?

points.p: Inadvertent damage to or removal of the parathyroids
points.why: They sit on the back of the thyroid.

points.p: Pseudo: end-organ resistance, GNAS G-protein defect
Complications: seizures, arrhythmia from long QT, laryngospasm, cataracts

glossary.PTH: Parathyroid hormone; raises blood calcium and makes the kidney excrete phosphate.
glossary.hypocalcaemia: A low blood calcium, below about 2.2 mmol/L.
glossary.hyperphosphataemia: A high blood phosphate; in hypoparathyroidism the kidney cannot excrete it.
glossary.hypomagnesaemia: A low blood magnesium; it blocks PTH release and action.
glossary.thyroidectomy: Surgical removal of the thyroid gland.
glossary.parathyroid glands: Four small glands behind the thyroid that make PTH.
glossary.tetany: Involuntary sustained muscle spasm from irritable nerves.
glossary.carpopedal spasm: Spasm of the hands and feet, fingers flexed at the knuckles.
glossary.laryngospasm: Spasm of the vocal cords that can block the airway.
glossary.Chvostek's sign: Twitching of the face when the facial nerve is tapped in front of the ear.
glossary.Trousseau's sign: Carpal spasm when a BP cuff is inflated above systolic pressure.
glossary.pseudohypoparathyroidism: Body tissues resist PTH, so calcium is low despite a high PTH.
glossary.pseudopseudohypoparathyroidism: The skeletal look of pseudohypoparathyroidism with normal blood tests.
glossary.GNAS: Gene for a G-protein that relays the PTH signal; mutations cause PTH resistance.
glossary.G-protein: Signalling protein that passes a hormone's message inside the cell.
glossary.metacarpals: The long bones of the hand; short 4th and 5th suggest pseudohypoparathyroidism.
glossary.bone profile: Blood panel of calcium, phosphate, albumin and ALP.
glossary.QT interval: ECG time from start of QRS to end of T wave; long in hypocalcaemia.
glossary.QTc: QT interval corrected for heart rate.
glossary.calcium gluconate: IV calcium preparation used for acute symptomatic hypocalcaemia.
glossary.alfacalcidol: Active vitamin D analogue that works without PTH or renal activation.
glossary.calcitriol: 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D, the active hormone form of vitamin D.
glossary.colecalciferol: Plain vitamin D3; needs liver and kidney activation.
glossary.1-alpha-hydroxylase: Kidney enzyme, switched on by PTH, that makes active vitamin D.
glossary.25-hydroxyvitamin D: The storage form of vitamin D measured to check vitamin D status.
glossary.depolarisation: The change in membrane charge that fires a nerve or muscle cell.
glossary.cataracts: Clouding of the eye's lens; a chronic hypocalcaemia complication.
glossary.Graves' disease: Autoimmune hyperthyroidism; a reason for thyroidectomy.
glossary.multinodular goitre: An enlarged thyroid with many nodules.
glossary.recurrent laryngeal nerve: Nerve to the vocal cords that can be injured in thyroid surgery, causing hoarseness.
glossary.secondary hyperparathyroidism: High PTH responding to low calcium, for example in vitamin D deficiency.

technique.stem: A 47 year old woman had a total thyroidectomy 2 days ago. She now has tingling around her lips and in her fingers, and her hands go into spasm when a BP cuff is inflated. Investigations: adjusted calcium 1.78 mmol/L (2.20–2.60), phosphate 1.76 mmol/L (0.80–1.50), PTH 0.4 pmol/L (1.6–8.5).
technique.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

steps.x: Diagnosis after neck surgery with a bloods panel.
Neck surgery, perioral paraesthesia, Trousseau's sign; low calcium, high phosphate, low PTH.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Post-thyroidectomy **hypoparathyroidism**.

elim: Can cause low PTH, but surgery is the obvious cause and magnesium is not given.
Gives fever and tachycardia, not tetany.
Causes a **high** PTH and low phosphate.

steps.x: **A. Hypoparathyroidism.** Low calcium + high phosphate + low PTH after neck surgery = hypoparathyroidism.

technique.stem: A 52 year old man has had 2 days of tingling fingers and muscle cramps. He drinks 60 units of alcohol a week. Investigations: adjusted calcium 1.92 mmol/L (2.20–2.60), PTH 1.1 pmol/L (1.6–8.5), phosphate 1.52 mmol/L (0.80–1.50).
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate next investigation?

steps.x: Next investigation: what explains a low PTH in a heavy drinker?
Low calcium with inappropriately low PTH, no neck surgery, heavy alcohol use.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Magnesium**: hypomagnesaemia blocks PTH release.

elim: Pancreatitis causes hypocalcaemia but does not explain a low PTH.
For myeloma, which causes high calcium.
Localises overactive parathyroids, not underactive ones.

steps.x: **B. Serum magnesium.** Hypocalcaemia with low PTH and no surgery: check magnesium.

technique.stem: A 38 year old woman had a parathyroidectomy and thyroidectomy yesterday. She now has carpopedal spasm and facial twitching on tapping the cheek. Her pulse rate is 108 bpm and BP 122/76 mmHg. Investigations: adjusted calcium 1.62 mmol/L (2.20–2.60). ECG shows a prolonged QT interval.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
o: Watch and repeat calcium in 24 hours

steps.x: 'Initial management' of a symptomatic patient.
Severe symptomatic hypocalcaemia with ECG changes: an emergency.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **IV calcium gluconate** with cardiac monitoring.

elim: She is symptomatic with a long QT.

steps.x: **B. IV calcium gluconate.** Symptomatic or long QT: IV calcium gluconate.

technique.stem: A 12 year old boy has short stature, a round face and short 4th and 5th metacarpals. He has muscle cramps. Investigations: adjusted calcium 1.94 mmol/L (2.20–2.60), phosphate 1.84 mmol/L (0.80–1.50), PTH 24.0 pmol/L (1.6–8.5).
technique.q: Which is the most likely mechanism?

steps.x: Mechanism behind a high PTH with low calcium and a phenotype.
Classic phenotype; low calcium and high phosphate despite a **high** PTH.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Tissues ignore PTH: **pseudohypoparathyroidism** (GNAS).

elim: Phosphate would be low, and no skeletal phenotype.

steps.x: **C. End-organ resistance to PTH.** High PTH but acts as if absent = resistance.

practice.stem: A 51 year old woman had a total thyroidectomy for Graves' disease yesterday. She now has tingling around her mouth and cramps in her hands. Her pulse rate is 98 bpm, BP 126/80 mmHg and temperature 37.0°C. Investigations are shown.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Low calcium, high phosphate and low PTH after thyroidectomy is hypoparathyroidism. Laryngeal nerve injury gives hoarseness, not tetany.

steps.x: Diagnosis after neck surgery.
Post-op, perioral paraesthesia, cramps; low calcium, low PTH.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Hypoparathyroidism** from parathyroid damage.

elim: Gives weakness, not perioral tingling and spasm.
Fever, tachycardia and agitation, normal calcium.

steps.x: **B. Hypoparathyroidism.** Tingling after thyroidectomy: check calcium.

practice.stem: A 45 year old woman is reviewed on the ward the day after thyroidectomy because of tingling fingers. Her pulse rate is 92 bpm and BP 124/76 mmHg. A BP cuff is inflated above systolic pressure for 3 minutes.
practice.q: Which is the most likely finding?
practice.e: Inflating a cuff above systolic provokes carpal spasm in hypocalcaemia: Trousseau's sign. Facial twitching on tapping is Chvostek's.

steps.x: Finding on a named examination manoeuvre.

clues: BP cuff is inflated above systolic pressure
steps.x: Suspected post-op hypocalcaemia; cuff test is Trousseau's.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Carpal spasm** (Trousseau's sign).

elim: A cerebellar sign, not a cuff test result.
Not provoked by a BP cuff.
That is Chvostek's sign, from tapping the facial nerve.

steps.x: **D. Carpal spasm.** Cuff = Trousseau's (hand); tap = Chvostek's (face).

practice.stem: A 14 year old girl has cramps and tingling in her hands. She is short and has short 4th metacarpals. Her pulse rate is 80 bpm and BP 108/66 mmHg. Investigations are shown.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Short metacarpals with low calcium and high PTH is pseudohypoparathyroidism (PTH resistance). Pseudopseudo has the phenotype with normal bloods.

steps.x: Diagnosis from phenotype plus bloods.
Hypocalcaemic symptoms, classic phenotype, high PTH.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Pseudohypoparathyroidism.**
**C. Pseudohypoparathyroidism.** Phenotype + low calcium + high PTH = pseudo.

practice.stem: A 16 year old boy has short 4th and 5th metacarpals and short stature. His mother has pseudohypoparathyroidism. He has no cramps or tingling. His pulse rate is 72 bpm and BP 112/70 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Pseudopseudohypoparathyroidism has the skeletal phenotype with normal calcium, phosphate and PTH.

steps.x: Phenotype with normal bloods.
The look of pseudohypo, no symptoms, normal biochemistry.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Pseudopseudohypoparathyroidism.**
**C. Pseudopseudohypoparathyroidism.** Same phenotype, normal biochemistry = pseudopseudo.

practice.stem: A 49 year old woman has known hypoparathyroidism after neck surgery. She stopped her medication 2 weeks ago and now has palpitations and tingling. Her pulse rate is 96 bpm and BP 118/74 mmHg. Adjusted calcium is 1.74 mmol/L (2.20–2.60). ECG (see item resources).

visual.title: Rhythm strip
visual.caption: Sinus rhythm; measure the QT interval.

practice.q: Which is the most likely finding on the ECG?
practice.e: Hypocalcaemia prolongs the QT interval and risks arrhythmia. Short QT is hypercalcaemia; peaked T waves are hyperkalaemia.

steps.x: ECG finding in a biochemical disorder.
Low calcium after stopping treatment.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Prolonged QT.**
**C. Prolonged QT interval.** Low calcium: long QT; high calcium: short QT.

practice.stem: A 58 year old man with alcohol excess and chronic diarrhoea has muscle twitching. He has had no neck surgery. His pulse rate is 88 bpm and BP 130/82 mmHg. Investigations are shown.
practice.q: Which is the most likely cause of his hypoparathyroidism?
practice.e: Severe hypomagnesaemia impairs PTH release and causes functional hypoparathyroidism; calcium will not correct until magnesium is replaced.

steps.x: Cause of low PTH without surgery.
Low calcium, low PTH and very low magnesium in a drinker.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Hypomagnesaemia** suppresses PTH secretion.

elim: Possible, but the low magnesium explains it.

steps.x: **B. Hypomagnesaemia.** Low PTH, no scar: check and correct magnesium.

practice.stem: A 40 year old woman has had perioral tingling for a week, 6 weeks after a total thyroidectomy. Her pulse rate is 78 bpm and BP 120/78 mmHg. Chvostek's sign is positive.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate diagnostic investigation?
practice.e: Hypoparathyroidism is a biochemical diagnosis: bone profile with PTH, plus magnesium and vitamin D.

steps.x: Diagnostic test for suspected hypocalcaemia.
Post-surgical hypocalcaemia suspected.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Bone profile with PTH**: low calcium, high phosphate, low PTH.

elim: Imaging does not diagnose a hormone deficiency.
Checks her thyroxine dose, not calcium.

steps.x: **A. Bone profile and PTH.** Gold standard: bone profile + PTH.

practice.stem: A 62 year old woman with chronic hypoparathyroidism attends the ED with palpitations and hand spasms. Her pulse rate is 112 bpm irregular, BP 110/70 mmHg. Investigations: adjusted calcium 1.66 mmol/L (2.20–2.60).
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate immediate investigation?
practice.e: Severe hypocalcaemia causes QT prolongation and arrhythmia, so an immediate 12-lead ECG is needed.

steps.x: Immediate investigation in a symptomatic patient.
Severe hypocalcaemia with palpitations.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **12-lead ECG** for QT prolongation and arrhythmia.
**A. 12-lead ECG.** Severe hypocalcaemia: ECG now.

practice.stem: A 46 year old woman is 1 day after thyroidectomy. She has carpopedal spasm and positive Chvostek's sign. Her pulse rate is 106 bpm and BP 124/78 mmHg. Investigations are shown.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
practice.e: Acute symptomatic hypocalcaemia after thyroidectomy needs IV calcium gluconate. Oral calcium is for mild or chronic disease.

steps.x: Initial management of symptomatic hypocalcaemia.
Tetany after neck surgery.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **IV calcium gluconate.**

elim: She has tetany; waiting is unsafe.

steps.x: **A. IV calcium gluconate.** Tetany = IV calcium gluconate.

practice.stem: A 50 year old woman had hypoparathyroidism after thyroidectomy 6 months ago. Her parathyroid function has not recovered. She takes oral calcium alone and still has a low calcium. Her pulse rate is 74 bpm and BP 122/78 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate addition to her treatment?
practice.e: Without PTH, renal 1-alpha-hydroxylation fails, so active vitamin D (alfacalcidol or calcitriol) is given alongside calcium.

steps.x: Long-term add-on to calcium.
Permanent hypoparathyroidism, inadequate on calcium alone.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Active vitamin D** (alfacalcidol).
**A. Alfacalcidol.** No PTH: give active vitamin D with calcium.

practice.stem: A 55 year old man has mild hypocalcaemia found 4 weeks after neck surgery. He has occasional tingling but no spasm. Chvostek's sign is negative. His pulse rate is 70 bpm and BP 130/80 mmHg. Adjusted calcium 2.06 mmol/L (2.20–2.60); ECG normal.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
practice.e: Mild hypocalcaemia without tetany or ECG changes is treated with oral calcium; IV calcium gluconate is reserved for severe symptoms.

steps.x: Initial management of mild hypocalcaemia.
Mild, stable hypocalcaemia.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Oral calcium supplements.**
**E. Oral calcium supplements.** Mild/chronic: oral calcium; severe: IV gluconate.

practice.stem: A 44 year old woman has hypoparathyroidism after thyroidectomy. She has tingling of her fingers and lips. Her pulse rate is 90 bpm and BP 120/76 mmHg. Adjusted calcium is 1.82 mmol/L (2.20–2.60).
practice.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of her tingling?
practice.e: Low extracellular calcium lowers the threshold for depolarisation of nerve and muscle membranes, causing paraesthesia and tetany.

steps.x: Mechanism of neuromuscular irritability.
Low extracellular calcium.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Low calcium **lowers the depolarisation threshold**: spontaneous firing.
**D. Lowered nerve depolarisation threshold.** Low calcium = excitable nerves.
